cosmos.title: Webb maps a lopsided atmosphere on the hot Jupiter WASP-17b
cosmos.summary: Using JWST, researchers found that the atmosphere of WASP-17b, a giant planet about 1,300 light-years away, extends farther out on one side than the other, though its overall outline is still roughly circular. The team, co-led by Cornell and Bristol, applied a method called transmission strings to Webb data. It shows a hotter evening limb and a cooler morning limb, as heat-carrying winds would produce. The results closely match earlier theoretical predictions and models. This is a measurement of a known planet, not an extraordinary claim.
cosmos.thought: Hot-Jupiter atmospheres could only be described as a single averaged ring, with one temperature and size all the way around the planet's edge.
cosmos.finding: A new technique applied to JWST data resolves differences around the planet's limb, showing that WASP-17b's evening side is hotter and more extended than its morning side.
cosmos.why: It gives a more detailed 3D picture of how winds and heat shape exoplanet atmospheres, which improves the models used to interpret all JWST spectra.
cosmos.source: ScienceDaily (Nature Astronomy study; Cornell University and University of Brist

cosmos.title: First known green star found among nearby white dwarfs
cosmos.summary: Astronomers analyzing white dwarf stars have found what they say is the first star that would look green to human eyes. The study looked at the 151 known white dwarfs within about 65 light-years of Earth. An outside astrophysicist noted that the work uses existing data and may not change our understanding of white dwarfs, though it offers a useful new way to view them. It was published in RAS Techniques and Instruments.
cosmos.thought: Stars show only a narrow range of colors tied to temperature, and a truly green star was not expected to exist.
cosmos.finding: White dwarfs can glow in a wider range of hues than most stars, and one nearby example would look green to a human observer.
cosmos.why: It shows that stellar remnants have more varied appearances than expected, and upcoming surveys that will multiply the number of white dwarfs with spectra could turn up more.
cosmos.source: CNN (study in RAS Techniques and Instruments; University of Warwick)

cosmos.title: FAST radio telescope finds a starless hydrogen cloud that may be a 'dark galaxy'
cosmos.summary: Astronomers using China's FAST radio telescope found a compact cloud of hydrogen with no visible stars or galaxy around it. It could be one of the strongest candidates yet for an isolated dark galaxy. This is a candidate only. The listing I found gives no peer-review details, and a dark galaxy has not been confirmed. Other explanations for the cloud have not been ruled out in the material I reviewed.
cosmos.thought: Galaxies are defined by the stars they contain, and gas clouds without stars were expected to be rare or short-lived.
cosmos.finding: A compact, isolated hydrogen cloud with no detectable stellar counterpart is now being proposed as a strong dark-galaxy candidate, but it is not confirmed.
cosmos.why: If dark galaxies exist, they would show that some of the gas in the universe never formed stars, which would change how we count and model galaxy formation.

deep_past.title: A Bronze Age wreck off Turkey is billed as the oldest known shipwreck
deep_past.summary: Divers off Kekova Island in southern Turkey have recovered more than 30 clay jars (amphorae) and three stone anchors from a wreck. The team dates it to 4,400–4,700 years ago, in the Early Bronze Age. No wood survives, so radiocarbon dating wasn't possible. The date rests on matching the jars' shape to dated examples from Egypt and the Levant, and clay analysis points to workshops in the Jordan Valley. The "oldest in the world" label comes from the excavators and Turkey's culture ministry. The July preliminary report in the Journal of Maritime Archaeology describes the wreck only as carrying Early Bronze Age amphorae.
deep_past.thought: The oldest known shipwreck was a roughly 4,200-year-old wreck near the Greek island of Dokos, and the Kekova jars looked only a century or two old when first found.
deep_past.finding: Comparing the jar styles with dated finds near the Giza pyramids and in the Levant puts the Kekova wreck about 200 to 500 years earlier, though the date rests on pottery typology and the full excavation has not yet been
deep_past.why: If the dating holds, it gives a rare direct look at long-distance sea trade between the Levant, Anatolia and the Aegean in the age of the pyramids.
deep_past.source: CNN (reporting Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism and Akdeniz University te

deep_past.title: Japan's 7,300-year-old Kikai-Akahoya super-eruption left a more complicated human footprint than assumed
deep_past.summary: A Lund University–led international team re-examined how people in prehistoric Japan fared after the Kikai-Akahoya eruption, one of Earth's worst volcanic disasters. Their results give a more complex picture of population change than earlier accounts did. Coverage of the study summarizes it as a surprising twist, but the news summaries I could access give few specifics, so check the original paper for the data and methods.
deep_past.thought: A catastrophe on the scale of Kikai-Akahoya was assumed to have devastated or wiped out the prehistoric populations in its path.
deep_past.finding: The new analysis of population levels after the eruption shows effects that were more varied and less clear-cut than that simple story.
deep_past.why: Prehistoric records of how societies absorbed a major eruption are a useful test case for how human populations respond to sudden environmental shocks.
deep_past.source: Phys.org / ScienceDaily (study led by Lund University)

deep_past.title: Drone lidar finds previously unknown rock shelters in Australia's Blue Mountains
deep_past.summary: Archaeologists used drone-mounted lidar to scan the Blue Mountains west of Sydney, where sandstone cliffs, dense eucalyptus forest and deep valleys hide much of the landscape from ground surveys. The scans picked out rock shelters not previously recorded, and the coverage also mentions rock art. Lidar only shows candidate sites; archaeologists still have to check them on the ground. I could only see summary-level coverage, so details such as shelter counts and dates are not stated here.
deep_past.thought: Rugged, heavily forested terrain made a complete record of Aboriginal rock shelters in the Blue Mountains practically impossible to build on foot.
deep_past.finding: Laser scanning from drones can see through the canopy and flag shelters that earlier surveys missed.
deep_past.why: Cheap drone lidar could speed up the mapping and protection of Indigenous heritage sites in places that are hard to reach.

reality.title: Webb finds an ancient galaxy cluster packed with more dark matter than models expect
reality.summary: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope has imaged a very early galaxy cluster. It holds an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter and seems to have formed sooner than current theories predict. The team also found a link between faint scattered starlight inside the cluster and the unseen dark matter. If other clusters show the same link, that starlight could become a way to map dark matter across cosmic history.
reality.thought: Massive, dark-matter-dominated galaxy clusters should take a long time to assemble, so very young ones should be rarer and less dense.
reality.finding: Webb sees an early cluster that is already heavy with dark matter, and its diffuse intracluster starlight appears to trace that hidden mass.
reality.why: It tests how quickly cosmic structure can form, which is a foundation of the standard model of cosmology. It also hints at a new way to map dark matter, which can't be seen directly. This is one cluster, so it challenges current models without overturning them.

reality.title: The universe may be 'stuck' in its current state, a new theoretical study suggests
reality.summary: Researchers modeled how a quantum field interacts with its surroundings during the rapid expansion of the early universe. They found a mechanism that makes a transition out of the universe's present state much less likely. The mechanism resembles the effects physicists study when trying to protect fragile information inside quantum computers. This is a theoretical result, so it has not been tested by observation.
reality.thought: The universe's current state might be only precariously stable, and quantum fluctuations could in principle tip it into a different state.
reality.finding: A model of an early-universe quantum field coupled to its environment suggests that interaction can lock the universe into its present state and suppress such a transition.
reality.why: It links quantum-computing ideas about protecting information to questions about the long-term stability of the cosmos. It is still a model, not an observed fact.

beyond.title: Ex-Pentagon UAP task force chief says he has seen non-human beings and craft
beyond.summary: Jay Stratton, the first director of the Pentagon's UAP Task Force, published a memoir on October 13 and has been giving TV interviews about it. He says the US government holds non-human craft and that he personally saw craft and beings. He also says a decades-long secrecy system keeps this from the public and from presidents. No physical evidence has been presented. Two former Senate investigators who dealt with him told the outlet Paradigm they did not recall him giving them information about alleged craft retrievals or reverse-engineering.
beyond.thought: Stratton says the US government possesses non-human craft and that he has personally seen non-human beings, with the truth hidden by an 80-year cover-up.
beyond.finding: No documents, physical evidence or independent corroboration have been produced, and former Senate investigators told Paradigm they did not recall him telling them about retrievals or reverse-engineering.
beyond.why: The claims come from a former senior defense intelligence official, were made in a book launch and TV interviews (CNN, Fox News), and have sparked a public dispute with another former UFO investigator.

beyond.title: Documentary says newly found 1966 film shows Bigfoot footage was staged
beyond.summary: The documentary Capturing Bigfoot presents a reel of 16mm film found in a safe. The reel reportedly shows about 40 seconds of a figure in a wooded area, dated to 1966, a year before the 1967 Patterson–Gimlin film. The film also includes interviews with Roger Patterson's son, who says his mother told him the footage was a hoax. Newsweek notes that the new material does not by itself settle the long dispute, and Bob Gimlin has continued to deny any staging.
beyond.thought: the documentary says the famous 1967 Patterson–Gimlin Bigfoot film was staged, and that the 1966 reel was a rehearsal for it.
beyond.finding: The reel and family accounts strengthen the case that the footage was staged, but Newsweek says they do not conclusively resolve the dispute, Gimlin denies a hoax, and Bigfoot's existence has never been scientifically established.
beyond.why: The 1967 film is the best-known piece of alleged Bigfoot evidence, and the documentary becomes available to rent on the film's anniversary, October 20.

beyond.title: Viral claim of an 11,000-year-old lost city under Turkey's Lake Van
beyond.summary: Divers filmed a stone wall, steps and a circular structure in Lake Van. Researcher Matthew LaCroix, quoted in the Daily Mail, suggests the remains could be at least 11,700 years old, possibly far older, and may be part of something much larger. Hürriyet Daily News reports his age estimate rests on interpretations of local geology and volcanic activity rather than direct archaeological dating. Other researchers have suggested the ruins date to the Urartian period about 3,000 years ago, or to the medieval era. Archaeologist Ömer Tanyürek, who dived there, says the 11,000-year claim is not supported by current evidence.
beyond.thought: a diving team says submerged stonework in Lake Van is an 11,000-year-old or older lost civilization, and some coverage links it to Noah's flood.
beyond.finding: Archaeologist Ömer Tanyürek, who dived the site, says the evidence does not support an 11,000-year-old civilization and that a medieval date is possible but preliminary, and Hürriyet reports no archaeological evidence confirms the older dat
beyond.why: Tabloid headlines tied the ruins to the Noah's Ark story and an ancient lost civilization, and the claim spread widely online.
beyond.source: Yahoo News (republishing GEEKSPIN); Hürriyet Daily News
